articles.title: Discussions of Race in Online Right-Wing Communities: A Cross-platform Computational Analysis of Reddit, Telegram, and Truth Social Using BERT and Structural Topic Modeling
articles.authors: Qin Li, Jack Gabriel Risien Wippell, Jasmine Hunt, Robert Bond, Joseph Tien, Nicole Yadon
articles.abstract: Race has long been a divisive fault line in American public discourse. Yet, political and societal changes have catalyzed the emergence of alternative collective identities, particularly in digital environments where alternative narratives can flourish. We examine right-wing social media spaces as forums in which racial discourse (specifically, that related to Black identities) is produced and contested through conversation, focusing on three platforms—Reddit, Truth Social, and Telegram—during Summer 2022. Structural topic modeling reveals six prominent themes: comparisons of the Black Lives Matter and January 6th protests; persistent discussions of race, crime, and violence; perceived racism within the Democratic party; broad discussion about ``wokeness''; race and health issues (abortion and infectious disease); and racial identity. While their relative prominence and framing vary, these themes appear across all three platforms. This indicates that racial narratives do not vary substantially across platforms. By extending the scope of social media platforms studied and foregrounding everyday conversations about race, this study advances academic understanding of how racial identities are both (re-)constructed and (re-)enforced online. In doing so, this study offers insights for political psychologists concerned with identity and its social underpinnings, as well as for scholars of race, political communication, culture, and collective behavior.

articles.title: Research on Han Nationalism in China in the 2020s (IV): Why Chinese Scholars Rarely Discuss Han Nationalism
articles.abstract: This article is one of a series of papers examining Han nationalist ideology in China in the 2020s. It seeks to explore the phenomenon whereby discourse related to Han nationalism has increased in Chinese online space in recent years, yet has rarely been treated as an independent object of inquiry within China’s mainstream social-science research system. The article argues that this phenomenon does not simply stem from a lack of scholarly attention, but is related to the operating environment of Chinese social science. Analyzing academic tradition, research frameworks, academic norms, the functions of think tanks, and the situation of scholars, the article points out that Chinese social-science research has long been shaped by existing theoretical systems, modes of resource allocation, and traditions of policy research, making it relatively difficult for certain issues involving ethnic identity, historical memory, and identity competition to form independent research paths. The article further discusses the distance between theoretical systems and public discourse, and how this structure affects the explanatory capacity of Chinese social science with respect to social currents such as Han nationalism. The article does not attempt to provide statistical estimates of the scale or social support for Han nationalism in China; rather, it seeks to pose a question: when a social idea enters the space of public discussion, why does the existing academic system find it difficult to explain the phenomenon adequately?

articles.title: Research on Han Nationalism in China in the 2020s (III): From Banner Affiliation to Ethnicity—The Reconstruction of Modern Manchu Identity and Online Narratives of Manchu–Han Conflict
articles.abstract: This article examines the formation of modern Manchu identity and its relationship to Manchu–Han tensions within the context of Han nationalist discourse on the Chinese internet in the 2020s. It begins by analyzing the Qing Eight Banner system, arguing that the banners were not a single-ethnicity organization in the modern sense, but a political and social system composed of multiple identity groups including Manchu, Mongol, Han-martial (Hanjun), and bondservant (baoyi) populations. After the fall of the Qing, the former banner affiliation was gradually reorganized within the modern ethnic classification system, producing the Manchu identity of today. The article further discusses the process of reconstituting modern Manchu identity since the 1980s, contending that this process involves both historical continuity and the influence of ethnic policy, local administrative factors, and practical interests. When ethnic identity becomes linked to the allocation of public resources, social policy, and historical narrative, it may shift from cultural identification toward an identity of social interest. The article maintains that contemporary Manchu–Han contradictions are not purely ethnic conflicts, but the product of the combined operation of historical memory, identity recognition, class differences, and material interests. Reducing the binding between ethnic identity and the distribution of public goods, thereby allowing ethnic identity to return more fully to the domain of cultural identification, may be an important direction for alleviating related tensions.

articles.title: Research on Han Nationalism in China in the 2020s (I): Examining the Narrative Contest between Han Nationalism and State Nationalism through the Withdrawal of the Film The Battle of Penghu
articles.abstract: Taking the withdrawal of the 2026 film The Battle of Penghu as a point of entry, this article explores the rise of Han nationalist ideology within Chinese society in the 2020s, and the increasingly prominent divergences in orientation between it and the officially led “Chinese nationalism (state nationalism).” The article analyzes the institutional roots of Han nationalism during a period of economic zero-sum competition, its contestation of historical narratives in the sphere of popular culture, and its comprehensive deconstruction of the official discursive system on core issues such as the definition of the nation, historical orthodoxy, and territorial legality.

articles.title: Research on Han Nationalism in China in the 2020s (II): Cultural Products, Historical Memory, and the Narrative Conflicts of Zhonghua Nationalism
articles.abstract: This paper examines how the narrative of Zhonghua nationalism exerts influence over cultural production in contemporary China and analyzes its structural ramifications. Within film and television, specific historical themes are constrained from entering mainstream cultural production; in video games, certain historical factions are minimized or rendered entirely absent from narratives; in online literature, market mechanisms reflect historical preferences distinct from official state narratives through reader subscription behavior; in historical publications, ethnicity-inflected linguistic expressions from the past undergo textual revision; and within the Hanfu movement, Han culture is not directly suppressed but rather subsumed and repackaged within the overarching framework of "Zhonghua culture."

articles.title: Everyday Talk and Child Development: A Conceptual Framework for the Informal Conversation Deficit Hypothesis A Theoretical Paper Proposing an Untested Hypothesis and Research Agenda
articles.abstract: Over recent decades, documented shifts in family and community routines — including declining rates of children walking to school, smaller household sizes, and increasingly structured extracurricular scheduling — have measurably reduced the settings in which children once encountered casual, unscripted conversation with a range of adults and peers. This paper proposes the term informal conversation deficit to describe a hypothesized reduction, alongside these routine changes, in children's everyday practice with varied social speech. The framework is motivated by the author's own long-standing personal observations, made over approximately five decades, of apparent declines in children's verbal and nonverbal (for example, body-language-based) social communication. These observations are offered as motivating context only: the paper presents no empirical data of its own, and every causal relationship it proposes is a hypothesis rather than an established finding. Drawing on Vygotsky's (1978) account of private speech, Romeo and colleagues' (2018) finding that conversational turns are associated with language-related brain function, and the ongoing debate over socioeconomic disparities in children's verbal environments, the paper considers how reduced frequency and variety of conversational practice may plausibly be linked to slower pragmatic language development and, in turn, to difficulty articulating internal states such as fear, frustration, or unmet needs. It is hypothesized that resulting frustration may sometimes present as behavior that resembles or compounds features of neurodevelopmental conditions, without being caused by them. The paper closes with explicit limitations and a proposed longitudinal study — using LENA audio-recording metrics — designed to test, for the first time within this framework, the relationship between conversational-turn exposure and children's emotional self-regulation

articles.title: Exposure to Heat Stress Influences Educational Outcomes in Low- and Middle-Income Countries
articles.authors: J. Huntley Compton, Brian C. Thiede
articles.abstract: Environmental stressors have widespread and multi-dimensional impacts on human population dynamics and wellbeing. A large literature has attempted to measure the effects of environmental shocks on human capital formation, including through studies of child nutrition and development, and there is growing interest in measuring environmental and climatic impacts on educational attainment itself. We advance this literature by linking data from the Multiple Indicator Cluster Surveys with district-level temperature records to measure the effects of heat exposures on educational outcomes across 29 countries. We assess both the medium-term and near-contemporaneous impacts of heat exposures. First, we evaluate how exposures from early life through age 14 are associated with the number of years of completed education among children ages 15-17 (n=307,614). Second, we measure the association between recent heat exposures and current school attendance among 5-17 year-olds (n=1,877,022). Temperature anomalies during the prenatal year through age 4 and between ages 10-14 are both associated with meaningful reductions in education by ages 15-17, with exposures to anomalies of +2 reducing education by 1.5-2.9 years (or approximately 28-53%). Recent temperature exposures were not associated with enrollment among 5-9 and 10-14 year-olds but unexpectedly increased the probability that 15-17 year-olds were enrolled in school. These results suggest that older children’s education may be protected against shocks in the short run but undermined by previous impacts on developmental and economic processes that unfold over multiple years.

articles.title: Covariate Adjustment in Political Science Experiments: Progress and Recommendations
articles.authors: Matthew H. Graham, Binh H Hoang
articles.abstract: Covariate adjustment can reduce the standard error of experimental treatment effect estimates without increasing the sample size but is vulnerable to abuse unless a specific procedure is preregistered. We assess adjustment practices in ten political science journals in 2013, 2018, and 2023-24. Encouragingly, preregistration and covariate adjustment have each been rapidly adopted. Preregistration is also a good predictor of what practices are used in articles. However, just 12% of articles published in 2023-24 preregister a specific covariate adjustment procedure and use adjustment for the main estimate. Although preregistering an adjusted estimator is not always advisable (when covariates are unavailable or preregistration is not possible), there is substantial room for improvement. We recommend that when feasible, researchers preregister a specific covariate adjustment procedure and use it for their preferred estimate regardless of covariate balance. This may require a shift in preregistration culture away from predicting results and toward constraining analysis.

articles.title: Beyond the Right Answer: Measuring Ethical Logic in Large Language Models
articles.abstract: Research on the ethical capacities of large language models has expanded rapidly, but the field remains conceptually fragmented. Some studies ask whether models agree with human moral judgments. Others examine moral values, developmental schemas, contextual norm recognition, resistance to framing, behavior under incentives, multimodal moral salience, or the perceived quality of model-generated advice. These approaches are often grouped under broad labels such as AI ethics, moral alignment, or moral reasoning, even though they measure substantially different constructs. This field is also distinct from much of the larger domain of LLM benchmarking because ethics does not generally provide ground truths that permit simple calculations of percent correct. This article reviews an expanded inventory of assessment families designed to evaluate how large language models respond to ethical choices. Building on early reviews such as Snoswell, Kilov, and Lazar (2026), this article treats the assessment family rather than the individual paper as the unit of analysis. It organizes the literature into five ethical measurement (ETHMEAS) dimensions: moral reasoning structure, moral value orientation, alignment with human values, contextual norm understanding, and behavior, harm, and social reception. The review also identifies a separate but increasingly important mechanistic-interpretability literature that attempts to locate moral concepts, values, and ethical-framework pathways inside model activations. The central claim is that the field is moving from outcome matching toward a more demanding investigation of ethical logic: the reproducible organization of moral attention, value prioritization, principle application, exception handling, justification, and conduct across changes in framing, language, context, modality, incentives, and internal intervention. A key conclusion is that a better understanding of the dynamics of LLM ethical logic informs our understanding of human ethical logic. The review identifies recurring validity challenges, including the transplantation of human psychometrics to language models, benchmark contamination, instability of model values, conflation of majority agreement with moral competence, and uncertainty about the relationship between explanations and underlying decision processes. ETHMEAS is proposed as a multidimensional framework for evaluating model ethical logic without reducing morality to a single score.

articles.title: Seeds of Change: Structural Transformations and Support for the Radical Right
articles.authors: Philipp Kerler, David Doyle, Victor Araújo
articles.abstract: The rise of the radical right is often attributed to economic disappointments rooted in structural transformations. However, these explanations frequently fail to extend beyond advanced democracies, where most structural changes differ. To advance the limited understanding of the political effects of structural transformations in countries of the Global South, we study the shift to high-intensity agricultural production in Brazil in the early 2000s. We argue that -- similar to electoral realignment in advanced democracies -- left majoritarian parties (in this case, the Brazilian Workers' Party, PT) losing the support of those left behind by structural change contributed significantly to Jair Bolsonaro's rise to power. At the same time, Bolsonaro's neoliberal appeals around revoking land protection and reducing trade barriers resonated with workers and farmers embedded in increasingly industrialized, export-oriented agriculture. Therefore, Bolsonaro garnered support from the winners and losers of structural transformation simultaneously. Contrary to the protectionist appeals of the radical right in the Global North, our research highlights the distinct role of neoliberal appeals for the success of the radical right in the Global South.

articles.title: Identity as Recognized Rather Than Constructed: Resonant Identity Theory and a Proposed Construct of Field State
articles.abstract: Chronic self-referential questioning of identity persists across the interventions designed to resolve it and frequently intensifies with the acquisition of self-knowledge. This paper argues that the persistence is structural, not incidental. Six influential accounts of identity, existentialist, cognitive, achievement-oriented, contemplative, status-based and narrative, differ substantially from one another while sharing the assumption that identity is constructed by the person whose identity it is. A construction that generates its own specification while executing it has no terminating condition, which is what a self-authored identity is. Resonant Identity Theory proposes the alternative: that identity is recognized rather than constructed, and that felt resonance functions as an instrument for self-knowledge rather than merely as an epiphenomenon of it. The ontological claim is acknowledged to be untestable. What is testable is the apparatus it generates. Field state is proposed as a construct describing the current relationship between recognized identity and its expression, distinct from trait profile, self-concept clarity and endorsed values, and operationalized through informant-rated cross-context consistency rather than self-report, on the grounds that the theory itself predicts self-report will fail in precisely the conditions it most needs to detect. Discriminant and falsification conditions are specified, including the finding most likely to refute the theory: if excavated self-relevant content skews toward moral approval, resonance is an approval detector and the epistemological claim fails. No empirical test has been conducted. The author declares a commercial interest in the framework.

articles.title: The Cultural Integration of Wellbeing Practices (CIWP) Framework: Conditions of Possibility Through Design
articles.abstract: The gap between knowing about wellbeing and practicing it constitutes a central challenge for research in design and public health. This article proposes the Cultural Integration of Wellbeing Practices (CIWP) Framework, a conceptual framework developed through Research through Design that articulates five dimensions—connection with meaningful values, situated opportunities, appropriation, everyday sustainability, and social legitimacy—to understand the conditions that support the incorporation of evidence-based wellbeing practices into everyday life and, eventually, into culture. Through a retrospective reading of the Wellbeing Practices in Waiting Spaces (WPWS) Framework, the article shows how these conditions can be translated into concrete design decisions through a situated activation mechanism, operationalized through three interdependent components—spatiotemporal conditions, human capacities, and visual mediation devices—and five design principles. The crosswalk indicates that WPWS provides direct operational expression to three of the five CIWP dimensions—situated opportunities, appropriation, and everyday sustainability—while connection with meaningful values and social legitimacy remain open dimensions that require processes beyond the visual mediation device itself. CIWP is offered as a transferable conceptual architecture—not as a fixed configuration—whose value will be tested through future operationalizations in contexts other than waiting spaces. Keywords: cultural integration of wellbeing practices; conditions of possibility; salutogenesis; interdisciplinarity for wellbeing; design for wellbeing promotion; Trauma-informed design; Research through Design; situated activation.

articles.title: Measuring Christian Nationalism: The Value of Self-Identification
articles.authors: Amy Grauley, Zachary Lien, Alena Smith, Priscilla Ziegler
articles.abstract: Scholars typically measure Christian nationalism (CN) using agreement with policy positions or statements linking Christianity to American identity, yet rarely consider whether individuals explicitly self-identify as Christian nationalists. This paper evaluates the analytic value of self-identification by comparing it to scale-based measures of CN. Using data from the Cooperative Election Study (CES), the Public Religion Research Institute (PRRI), and open-ended survey responses, we distinguish between individuals who self-identify as Christian nationalists, those who score high on CN scales but reject the label, and those who reject CN as both an identity and a worldview. We show that CN identity and CN belief are related but distinct, and that self-identification matters most when CN belief is low. Among low-belief respondents, adopting the CN label is associated with markedly different political attitudes, while at high levels of CN belief, identity adds little explanatory power beyond belief. These findings highlight limits of worldview-based measures and demonstrate the value of incorporating identity into the study of Christian nationalism.

articles.title: CHALLENGES AND OPPORTUNITIES FOR DEVELOPING UPCYCLED COSMETIC INGREDIENTS IN BRAZIL: A PERSPECTIVE FOR SMALL AND MEDIUM ENTERPRISES
articles.authors: Murilo Dotti Garcia, Orlando Nastri Neto
articles.abstract: The use of plant by-products to develop cosmetic ingredients has gained considerable momentum globally, driven by growing demand for sustainability and the increasing expectation that ingredients deliver scientifically proven efficacy. Brazil offers particularly favourable conditions for this trend, since the country combines unparalleled biodiversity with a world-scale agribusiness chain that generates vast volumes of largely underused by-products. This article examines the main challenges and opportunities facing Brazilian small and medium cosmetic enterprises (SMEs) as they develop ingredients from these by-products, focusing on regulatory, technical, scientific and market dimensions. Drawing on an integrative review of recent scientific and sectoral literature and on an analysis of the national context, it argues that SMEs, despite capital and infrastructure constraints, hold genuine advantages in agility and proximity to regional production chains. It concludes that conditions are favourable for smaller companies willing to invest in technical capacity, strategic partnerships and differentiation grounded in scientific evidence.

articles.title: Insufficiently Affordable: Public Opinion About Housing Affordability
articles.authors: Tali Mendelberg, Gustavo Novoa, Adrian C. Pietrzak

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: Americans want government to improve housing affordability. Yet proposals for affordable housing often encounter public resistance. We argue for a neglected explanation: concerns that these proposals are insufficiently affordable. Using four original surveys with novel, precise measures of affordability and randomized developer and landlord profiteering, we find wide support for affordable housing when it primarily benefits people of low means and does not favor developer or landlord profiteering. This support holds even when the hypothetical building is proposed in the respondent’s neighborhood, support entails tradeoffs and costly behavior in the survey, and the policy requires tax increases. The tax finding replicates in election outcomes of actual ballot measures. Pro-poor sentiments shape these preferences, above and beyond self-interest, and offset the negative impact of racial attitudes. Buildings and policies that satisfy these sentiments draw much higher public support. However, common policies fail to do so.

articles.title: The Politics of Consolidation: Authoritarian Drift and Economic Ambition in Post-Election Tanzania
articles.abstract: Abstract Tanzania’s political trajectory in August 2026 is increasingly defined by a striking contradiction: ambitious economic modernization is unfolding alongside a marked contraction of political space. Following the contested October 2025 general election, President Samia Suluhu Hassan’s administration appears increasingly focused on restoring political control while facing unresolved questions concerning electoral legitimacy, accountability and constitutional reform (BBC, 2026; Xinhua, 2026a; Xinhua, 2026b). The resignation of Vice President Emmanuel Nchimbi on 25 August 2026 (BBC, 2026; KBC Digital, 2026), restrictions on opposition political activity (The Citizen, 2026b; Daily News, 2026a), and the prosecution of opposition leader Tundu Lissu (The Citizen, 2026a; Mwananchi, 2026) have intensified concerns about the direction of Tanzania’s political order. At the same time, major infrastructure achievements, particularly the Julius Nyerere Hydropower Project, provide the government with a powerful narrative of developmental competence (Xinhua, 2026c). This paper situates these developments within the comparative literature on democratic backsliding, electoral authoritarianism, political legitimacy, institutional change and developmental states. Drawing on Bermeo’s (2016) analysis of democratic backsliding, Schedler’s (2013) conception of electoral authoritarianism, Beetham’s (1991) theory of political legitimacy, and Doner, Ritchie, and Slater’s (2005) analysis of developmental states, it argues that Tanzania is exhibiting features of political consolidation in which executive control and developmental performance increasingly operate as mutually reinforcing sources of regime stability. The paper does not suggest that Tanzania has become a fully authoritarian state. Rather, it identifies an authoritarian drift in which restrictions on political competition and civic space coexist with continued electoral institutions and ambitious economic modernization. The central argument is that economic performance may strengthen short-term regime legitimacy, but it cannot permanently substitute for credible elections, accountable institutions, judicial independence and meaningful political inclusion. The widening gap between developmental ambition and political openness consequently represents both a democratic challenge and a long-term governance and investment risk.

articles.title: Perceived Benefits of a Cosmetology-Based Self-Care Program for Family Caregivers of Older Adults with Cognitive Decline: An Exploratory Qualitative Study
articles.authors: Riko Nakayama, Hana Sakurai, Fumiko Miyamae, Mutsuko Okamura, Chiaki Ura, Tsuyoshi Okamura, Tomoko Wakui
articles.abstract: Background: Family caregivers of older adults with cognitive decline often have limited opportunities for self-care. Objective: This study explored the perceived benefits of a cosmetology-based self-care program for family caregivers of community-dwelling older adults with cognitive decline. Methods: A qualitative descriptive study was conducted with family caregivers in a community setting in Tokyo, Japan. Participants attended a cosmetology-based session that included light physical activity, skincare, and makeup. Data were collected using free-response questionnaire and focus group interviews and analyzed using inductive content analysis. Results: Eight family caregivers were included in the analysis. Inductive qualitative content analysis identified three main categories: (1) emotional relief and enjoyment through shared experience, (2) heightened self-awareness and reorientation toward the self, and (3) emerging motivation for self-care and reframing of caregiving. Participants described relaxation, recognition of accumulated fatigue and neglected personal needs, and reassurance and connection through interactions with other caregivers.

articles.title: Institutional Voice Laundering: Multimodal Risks and a Benchmark for Civic Fidelity
articles.abstract: Public institutions are increasingly being designed in forms that Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems can process easily, sometimes before those forms are equally clear to citizens. People increasingly encounter ministries, hospitals, regulators, and courts through AI-mediated summaries, translations, voice interfaces, and visual reformulations, often before seeing the original communication itself. This paper argues that such mediation can weaken important features of institutional communication. Public messages that were originally attributable and open to scrutiny may be recast as apparently neutral assistance, while losing cues about jurisdiction, uncertainty, evidence, and avenues for appeal, even when the output appears fluent and useful. To frame this problem, two linked concepts are introduced here: (1) the machine-readable institution and dual legibility; and (2) a Civic Fidelity Index to assess how much civic meaning is preserved when institutional communication is transformed by AI. This problem is fundamentally multimodal, because many failures arise not from text paraphrase alone but from the way information is reformulated across text, speech, images, and interface elements. We identify research directions around multimodal fidelity, reversible mediation, cross-lingual robustness, and no-laundering standards for accountable AI.

articles.title: NEXUS-HC: A Framework for Technology Foresight in Strategic Communications
articles.abstract: This conference paper introduces NEXUS-HC (Navigational Examination and Understanding System for Hype Cycle Analysis), a decision-oriented framework for technology foresight in strategic communications. The framework adapts the familiar hype-cycle concept for contested, next-generation information environments shaped by automation, synthetic media, algorithmic information operations, AI avatars, and emerging influence technologies. It standardises technology assessment through a lightweight cross-impact rubric and links assessment outcomes to five portfolio postures: Monitor, Pilot, Adopt, Govern/Harden, or Counter. NEXUS-HC is designed to help strategic communications teams compare emerging technologies, record evidence and confidence levels, set reassessment triggers, and brief leaders using a transparent and auditable decision record. This is the published conference proceedings paper from the Proceedings of the 25th European Conference on Cyber Warfare & Security (ECCWS 2026). The official version of record is available at https://doi.org/10.34190/eccws.25.1.4709.

articles.title: Legitimacy Without Exit: Why Voluntary Alternatives to the State Lose to Involuntary Ones
articles.abstract: Discourse on the future of the state usually treats voluntary alternatives (network states, micronations, charter cities) and involuntary reconfigurations of political identity (civilizational-state rhetoric, corporate infrastructural control) as one phenomenon — "the state losing its monopoly." This paper argues the frame conflates two structurally different processes and proposes a testable thesis: a new political container's durable legitimacy — from an offshore platform to a state itself — depends not on the voluntariness of its formation, but on whether it inherits an existing power's legitimating apparatus, secures that power's patronage, or independently builds comparable governance competence. The thesis is tested on controlled comparisons rather than mismatched object types: unpatronized claimants (Sealand, Republic of Minerva, Liberland, Próspera, Ciudad Morazán) against patronized de facto states of the same type (Abkhazia, Transnistria, Northern Cyprus), backed by a systematic dataset of all 34 de facto states, 1945–2011, including the author's own reanalysis of its raw data, and re-tested on an independent second dataset (Kursani, 2023) where patronage showed no statistical link to legitimacy. A further check replacing a blunt democracy proxy with a variable matching the paper's own institutional argument (party-ban severity, V-Dem data) found the regime-type confound more robust, not less — reported honestly rather than as a convenient result. Negotiated decolonization is compared with unilateral declarations of independence across three post-communist federations (Bunce, 1999) and illustratively via Rhodesia and the 2023–2024 collapse of Nagorno-Karabakh, where patron withdrawal itself proved to be a product of internal delegitimation inside the patron state. For micronations, lacking any peer-reviewed dataset, the paper builds its own coding of all 81 documented cases (0/81 with a patron, 0/81 with confirmed recognition). Two cases the mechanism explains only partially are addressed directly: the USSR's collapse despite one of history's highest documented exit costs, and the breakdown of Sweden's neo-corporatist model. The causal mechanism (Weberian legitimacy via Hirschmanian exit/voice/loyalty) is marked as interpretation, not fact, and is empirically hard to distinguish from simple patronized power; open survey data on four de facto states offers a first partial, substantive test of this distinction. The thesis is probabilistic, not universal: no single future case falsifies it — a pattern across independent cases is required. The paper addresses three potential counterexamples (neo-corporatism, EU constitutional patriotism, universal basic income) and twelve explicitly unresolved debates, presenting none as settled consensus.

articles.title: From Silence to the Archive: The Uneven Institutionalization of Legal-Political Memory Across Displacement Contexts
articles.abstract: Legal-political memory occupies an ambivalent position in contexts marked by state violence and forced migration: documentation promises evidentiary weight, yet producing it can expose the documenter to risk. Drawing on 80 semi-structured interviews with Kurdish-origin participants across three positional contexts (Bölge, n=25; İç Anadolu, n=25; Diaspora, n=30), coded against a reliability-tested framework (overall κ=0.838), this article examines Documentary Witnessing and Legal Memory (κ=0.818) and Institutional/Archival Memory and Digitization (κ=1.000). Documentary witnessing remains uniformly weak across contexts (8.0–13.3 per cent), while institutional memory diverges sharply, reaching 50.0 per cent among Diaspora participants against 16.0–20.0 per cent within Turkey. Read through Halbwachs, Assmann, Derrida and Trouillot, we read this pattern as consistent with a geography of risk rather than a uniform absence of institutions: within our sample, protective silence is most visible near the site of origin, material erosion under internal displacement, and institutionalization at greater distance. A cross-cutting family-archive practice further complicates the institutional/oral binary.

articles.title: Capital as a System of Multidimensional Valuations: Transformation, Money Crisis and Contours of New Architecture.
articles.abstract: The article is devoted to an analysis of the fundamental transformation of the nature of capital in the 21st century. Despite the growing body of research on intangible assets, debt dynamics, and the concentration of wealth, there is no comprehensive framework linking these trends to the crisis of money’s functions and the formation of a new capital architecture. Based on a comparison of aggregated data — the share of intangible assets in 92% of the capitalization of the S&P 500 (Ocean Tomo, 2025), global debt of $353 trillion (IIF, 2026), wealth concentration in 0.001% of the population (WIR, 2026) — and illustrative cases (capitalization of Tesla, dynamics of real estate prices in megacities, digital assets) it is shown that the dominant form of capital is shifting from material to a valuation system based on expectations, narratives and trust. Four key drivers of transformation are identified: technological, institutional, environmental, and socio‑psychological. The crisis of the four functions of money — as a measure of value, a medium of exchange, a store of value, and a means of payment — is interpreted as a symptom of a deeper shift in valuation. It is substantiated that money will retain its function as a measure of value even as the object of measurement changes — from physical goods and labour to data, algorithms, reputation, and trust. Three scenarios for a new capital architecture are formulated — energy‑based, digital, and institutional — and the need to transition to a multidimensional system of value assessment, which includes energy, data, trust, and natural capital, is substantiated.

articles.title: Action framing modulates the Pavlovian bias in go and no-go learning
articles.abstract: Reward- and punishment-associated (i.e., Pavlovian) cues can trigger specific responses that interfere with learning appropriate actions. For instance, several studies have shown that reward impedes the learning of no-go responses, while punishment impedes the learning of go responses. This so-called Pavlovian bias is theorized to arise at the motor level, and to reflect a tight or even “hardwired” coupling between reward and action activation, and between punishment and action suppression. Contrary to this view, across two experiments testing adults (one pre-registered, total N = 370), using behavioral analyses and computational modeling, we show that action framing strongly modulates Pavlovian bias. When go was framed as approach and no-go as avoidance, we replicated the typical asymmetry in learning. However, when go was framed as avoidance and no-go as approach, this Pavlovian bias in choice disappeared. Pavlovian bias thus operates partly on a semantic level, and is more flexible than often theorized.

articles.title: Natural Hazards Threat and Early Marriage for Women and Girls in Latin America and the Caribbean
articles.authors: Boyoon Lee, Guilherme N. Fasolin, Ted Hsuan Yun Chen

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: Natural hazards threat can shift marriage practices in ways that systematically harm young women and girls, as post-disaster conditions incentivize families to marry off daughters as an adaptation response against economic and physical insecurity. We study this link using geolocated representative samples from 15 countries in Latin America and the Caribbean, a region with one of the highest early marriage rates in the world. We show that exposure to natural hazards is associated with higher prevalence of marriage among women under 18 and increased acceptance of these marriage practices among the general population. This relationship is mitigated by strong government institutions, which was previously unobserved in other regions. Our study demonstrates that rational climate adaptation behaviors at the household level can exacerbate within-household distributional inequalities, emphasizing the need for stronger institutional support structures that provide equitable means of adaptation.

articles.title: Electricity Patronage and the Energy Transition: Indonesia in Comparative Perspective
articles.abstract: Governments across the Global South are choosing between clean electricity or fossil fuels. Electricity procurement regimes—the practices governing how governments and utilities allocate generation contracts and associated rents—are a critical and overlooked determinant of this choice. Using Indonesia as a theory-building case, I argue that the programmatic character of electricity procurement shapes whether governments can credibly commit to renewable energy producers, select least-cost projects, and provide the collective goods renewables require to scale. Patronage-based procurement regimes, in contrast, systematically favor fossil fuels. I trace Indonesia’s coal entrenchment to its patronage-based procurement regime, in which clientelist party competition, weak executive constraints, and failed reforms concentrated discretion in the state-owned utility PLN, which operated as a broker for the ruling coalition. Comparative cases in India and South Africa show how programmatic reforms enabled renewable scale-up despite similarly powerful fossil fuel incumbents. The findings advance a meso-level account that bridges the comparative politics literature on patronage and the study of global energy transitions.

articles.title: When voters take a stance: How voting on issues influences support for parties
articles.abstract: What are the consequences of referendums for voting for parties? Despite increased use of direct democratic instruments around the world, this question has been essentially ignored. I argue that referendums lead to a realignment between voters and parties that is consistent with a bidimensional model of proximity voting. The analysis of nine referendums that took place in seven countries between 2015 and 2025 confirm the predictions showing that, after each consulta-tion, a sizeable share of cross-pressured voters who cast a referendum vote against party recom-mendations “follow the issue”, switching to a party that is in line with their issue positions. Ideological proximity with parties, however, moderates vote switching. In highly salient consultations, this pattern persists over time. Further experimental evidence confirms the causal link between issue-based considerations and voting. These findings have relevant implications for how direct democracy impacts a fundamental aspect of democratic representation, namely voting for parties.

articles.title: ICT, Sustainable Development and Job Polarization: Evidence from ECOWAS
articles.abstract: This paper assesses the contribution of information and communication technology (ICT) to sustainable development and job polarization in the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS). Panel pooled mean group models are used to assess the role of ICT in sustainable development whereas changes in employment shares of the International Standard Classification of Occupations (ISCO08) occupations are used to investigate the changing employment distribution in the labor markets in the region. The results show that all measures of ICT had a positive and significant impact on sustainable development. The paper also finds that the West African countries are lagging in terms of ICT adoption and ICT infrastructure. The pace of adoption is slower compared to developed countries thus minimizing the pace of job polarization. The results obtained found no u-shaped employment distribution in the countries to indicate job polarization. Significantly however, there is a decline in the share of employment of the agriculture, forestry and fishery sectors. The decline in the share of employment is however offset by rising employment shares of most middle-skilled occupations in the region.

articles.title: When the Diagnosis Breaks the Home: Paternal Abandonment and Maternal Endurance in Families of Children with Disabilities in Bangladesh
articles.abstract: In Bangladesh, literature shows that a child with a disability is considered to profoundly reorient family life around the mother, who becomes the primary and often only caregiver. A smaller but growing body of research has also documented the financial hardship, institutional barriers, and religiously-inflected stigma that already accompany this caregiving role. An examination of a dimension that is not closely studied in the context of Bangladesh, a child’s disability in marriage dissolution of the parents, extends that literature. In keeping with the secondary qualitative methodology that Cheong et al. (2023) propose, the study analyses eight past news narratives (2016-2026) in Bangladeshi media, which are publicly available. In these narratives, family members speak for themselves about raising a disabled child. Discourse analysis reveals three themes. First, mothers globally carry the structural weight of caring for the family, regardless of the father’s involvement. Second, some discourse suggests the child’s disability is sometimes ‘responsible’ for the father’s exit, which can occur before and/or after birth. Third, despair for the future collides with maternal agency, best seen through the mother who established her own school after being turned away from every single one. The analysis does not imply a causal link between disability and divorce. It shows how this link is narrated in the Bangladeshi public sphere. The analysis offers the narrated link as a focused question for future primary, interview-based research. As an exploratory secondary analysis, this piece recognises the limitation of the data being drawn from credible journalistic sources rather than high-quality interviews.

articles.title: Position: A Score Should Travel With Its Repair History
articles.abstract: In machine learning a capability claim becomes established when a model outperforms its predecessors on benchmarks the community already accepts, and peer review confines itself to checking that those scores are reported and compared correctly. We argue that benchmarks consequently perform the adjudicating role that peer review performs in other sciences, and that the field has organised no stewardship to match, since a benchmark is reviewed once, when the paper introducing it is accepted, and never again during the years in which it serves as evidence. Our position is that this arrangement, which we call review once and use forever, is the first bottleneck a meta-science of AI research should address. We support the position with the public lifecycle of MMLU, the benchmark its successors describe as the de facto standard for general capability. Between 2024 and 2025 five independent projects repaired four distinct defects in MMLU, none of them by the original authors and none as part of any joint programme. A count across the benchmark paper, model reports, leaderboards and governance syntheses then shows the qualifications attached to an MMLU score falling from 2.4 per reporting event in the repair papers to 1.0 in frontier model reports, three in ten of which carry none. On this basis we propose three norms for venues, funders and governance bodies, and we answer the objection that unstewarded benchmarks have served the field well.

articles.title: Evaluating the Theory of the AnthroShift: How are Climate Shocks Related to Civic Engagement and Support for Climate Science in the US?
articles.abstract: Since the theory of the AnthroShift was introduced in 2019, it has been increasingly seen as a theoretical lens through which to analyze social responses to climate change. This paper builds on this small but growing literature to assess the AnthroShift at the individual level. We analyze a new dataset collected from a national sample of adults in the US to understand how experiencing climate shocks is associated with climate-change supportive attitudes and behaviors. Specifically, we look at how self-reported experiences with climate shocks are associated with heightened levels of civic engagement and support for the science that documents climate change. This paper is separated into three sections. First, we review the theory of the AnthroShift, which explains how risk pivots can drive environmental behaviors, and connect it with the growing research that assesses the social effects of climate shocks. Next, we describe our data, which were collected from a nationally representative sample of adults in the US in fall 2025 (n=1,068). Third, we present the results of our analysis that document how individuals’ experience with climate shocks is strongly associated with civic and political engagement and support for climate science. The paper concludes by discussing the implications of our findings for the relationship between climate shocks, attitudes, and behaviors, as well as for our understanding of the society-environment relationship and the sociological theory of the AnthroShift.

articles.title: When Belonging Comes Before Belief: Inherited Identity, Social Conformity, and the Difficulty of Looking Outside the Group
articles.abstract: People normally receive an identity before they are old enough to examine it. A child is born into a family, a language, a religious or non-religious environment, and a set of trusted authorities. By the time the person is able to compare different beliefs, one position already feels familiar and the others often feel foreign. This essay asks a simple social question: how much of what we defend comes from examination, and how much comes from belonging? The argument is not that inherited beliefs are false, or that following experts is irrational. It is that social identity can make some questions costly to ask. Family ties, community approval, reputation, and fear of exclusion can narrow the range of views people seriously examine. A recent personal example from British Muslim life is used to illustrate the problem: communities with access to the same modern information may still follow different inherited authorities when deciding religious dates. The wider point applies beyond religion. Political, national, family, and professional identities can work in the same way. The essay argues that genuine conviction is stronger when a person can examine alternatives without having to lose the social world to which he or she belon

articles.title: Research on Han Nationalism in China in the 2020s (VI): The Social Foundations, Core Demands, and Future Trajectory of Han Nationalism
articles.abstract: After 2020, discussions related to Han nationalism in Chinese online space have increased markedly and have gradually become an important topic for understanding contemporary Chinese ethnic identification, historical narratives, and social contradictions. As the final article in this series of studies, the present paper attempts, from the angles of demographic change, resource allocation, ethnic policy, and national identification, to analyze the social background of the emergence and development of Han nationalism. The article argues that Han nationalism does not simply originate from historical sentiment, but is a form of identity-political expression formed in the process of change in Chinese social structure. With the decline in birth rates, adjustments in the mode of economic growth, and increases in social competitive pressure, some groups have begun to reopen discussion of the fairness of ethnic policy, the boundaries of the national community, and the relations of responsibility and interest among different groups. The article further organizes the principal demands advanced by some Han nationalists, including the abolition of preferential policies based on ethnic identity, renewed discussion of relations of autonomy and fiscal transfer in ethnic regions, and the improvement of social security for lower- and middle-strata groups. At the same time, the article analyzes the possible positive effects of Han nationalism—for example, pushing long-neglected questions into public discussion, emphasizing the principle of civic equality, and strengthening the sense of social responsibility of the majority group. Yet the article also points out that this body of thought possesses potential risks such as ethnicizing complex social problems, neglecting intra-ethnic class differences, and intensifying logics of group competition. This article does not attempt simply to affirm or negate Han nationalism; rather, it hopes, by organizing its internal logic and social background, to provide an exploratory analytical framework for understanding changes in Chinese ethnic identification after 2020.

articles.title: Research on Han Nationalism in China in the 2020s (V): Three Frameworks for Interpreting Qing History—Han Nationalism, New Qing History, and Chinese Nationalism
articles.abstract: This article examines the differences that have arisen among Han nationalism, Chinese nationalism, and international New Qing History in the 2020s concerning the interpretation of Qing history. It argues that the three narratives do not revolve merely around evaluations of the Qing, but respectively focus on questions of ethnic identity, imperial structure, and the historical continuity of the modern state. Han nationalism emphasizes ethnic hierarchy and historical rupture under Qing rule; New Qing History places the Qing within a comparative framework of Eurasian empires and stresses its multi-ethnic imperial character; Chinese nationalism emphasizes the Qing’s important role in the formation of modern China’s territory and national community. The article further points out that controversies surrounding the Qing in fact reflect different understandings within contemporary Chinese society of national identification, ethnic relations, and the allocation of resources.

articles.title: When Full Employment Is No Longer Necessary

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: Artificial intelligence may reduce the economic necessity of some forms of cognitive labour faster than employment and social institutions can reorganize the time, identity and roles that work currently structures. Rather than forecasting mass unemployment, we ask what should be tested if that transition arrives unevenly or abruptly: how people are received after occupational loss, how newly available time becomes genuinely self-directed, whether AI can make heterogeneous, voluntary arrangements administratively feasible without turning personalization into obligation, whether unmet human needs can support voluntary new roles, and what it costs to keep the human last mile human. Employment organizes more than income, so occupational displacement is an institutional problem as well as an economic one. We set out a sequence — receive, stabilize, recover, choose — in which recovery is a legitimate state rather than a delay before activation, and in which voluntary reconnection is one possible exit among many. The central proposition is offered as a hypothesis rather than a finding: full employment may have functioned partly as a technology of standardization, while AI could make heterogeneity administratively affordable. Because the same capacity could also produce a more efficient workfare machine, we propose personalization without compulsory optimization as a governing constraint. AI may make matching cheap without making human contact cheap.

articles.title: Defaulting to Decarbonization? Financial Insolvency and the Energy Transition in India’s States

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: How do financial constraints shape the energy transition in developing countries? I study this question in India, where electricity procurement is governed at the subnational level. Electoral politics motivates state governments to subsidize electricity consumption, resulting in financial stress for electricity distribution utilities (DISCOMs). Using multiple sources of original data on utility and plant operations, I investigate the relationship between financial distress and decarbonization. I theorize that the effect of utility insolvency depends on the margin considered—dispatch vs. capacity investment—and on institutions. Counterintuitively, but consistent with my theory, I find that financial stress is associated in the short run with greater relative procurement of renewable energy and less procurement of fossil fuels. Mechanism tests suggest that coal dispatch is more sensitive to liquidity constraints, as distressed DISCOMs cut back on coal deliveries while renewable energy remains protected by “must-run” dispatch regulations. In contrast, I find at most weak evidence that insolvency raises challenges for decarbonizing electricity in the long run: insolvency shows no relationship with renewable-energy tendering, only suggestive evidence that it slows renewable capacity investment, and similarly weak evidence that it curtails expansion of transmission lines that renewables need to scale. The results qualify the conventional wisdom that electricity utility insolvency is a binding constraint on the energy transition.

articles.title: When Are Asymmetric Fixed-Effects Models Within-Person Tests of Reversibility? Heterogeneous Responses and Bidirectional Support
articles.abstract: Asymmetric fixed-effects models are increasingly used in sociological research to test whether an effect reverses when a time-varying predictor changes direction. Because these models rely on within-person change, directional asymmetry is often interpreted as evidence of within-person irreversibility. This study shows that this interpretation requires an additional cross-person homogeneity assumption. I reparameterize Allison’s (2019) cumulative asymmetric fixed-effects model exactly as a model of current state and total movement, revealing that the specification pools current-state responses across individuals. When those responses are heterogeneous and systematically related to who moves upward versus downward, pooled asymmetry can arise even when every individual’s response is perfectly reversible. I derive this mover-composition result and characterize what remains identifiable when individual state responses are unrestricted. A common path response—the additional response associated with accumulated movement conditional on current state—can then be identified only from within-person bidirectional movement, provided that the resulting variation is not absorbed by period effects. Monte Carlo simulations and a reanalysis of Allison’s wage example illustrate the resulting assumption–support–precision trade-off and show that relevant support depends on the structure of observed trajectories, not simply on the number of directional transitions.

articles.title: Greenhouse Gas Mitigation and Climate Change Adaptation: Some Policy Alternatives for Nepal
articles.abstract: Many scientists consider climate change to be the most important environmental issue of this century. Although some controversy lingers about the extent of anthropogenic contribution to global warming, most scientists and experts agree that, due to the increased greenhouse gases (GHG) in the atmosphere, Earth’s average temperature is gradually rising, and the ensuing climate change is causing significant and mostly negative impacts on the environment and human population. Various studies show that average global temperatures have already risen by 0.8 degrees Celsius over pre-industrial levels. Scientists estimate that at this rate, the average temperatures are likely to rise by at least about 2 degrees Celsius by the end of the century. It is widely believed that a rise of more than 2 degrees Celsius in the average global temperature can bring serious adverse impacts to the global ecosystem and human welfare.

articles.title: The alchemy linking “gender ideology,” left-wing authoritarianism, and political violence: Comment on Fedida et al.

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: In a report commissioned by the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, Fedida et al. (2026) analyze data from an opt-in nonprobability sample to describe associations among a newly developed five-item Clinical Gender Affirmation Scale (CGAS), scores on the Brief Left-Wing Authoritarianism Scale, and respondents’ justification of politically charged violent acts. Their interpretation, however, is that “gender ideology,” embedded in clinical guidance, supplies authoritarian psychology with enemies, moral urgency, and rationales for coercion. This commentary argues that the data and analyses do not support this conclusion. First, CGAS measures a narrow cluster of attitudes toward social affirmation and support, not the clinical-institutional ideology attributed to it. Second, Fedida et al. (2026) invoke selection, mediation, and effect-modification theories without specifying or testing them. In particular, an “ideological accelerant” hypothesis requires an interaction between CGAS and authoritarianism, but no such interaction is estimated. Third, the estimated associations are difficult to interpret because the measures contain overlapping ideological and aggression-related content, while the violence items assess reactions to a politically selective set of hypothetical targets rather than a generalized disposition to tolerate political violence. Moreover, modeling CGAS and left-wing authoritarianism in separate regressions adjusted only for political identity does not show that either is associated with justification of violence independently of the other. In summary, Fedida et al. (2026) describe potentially interesting covariances but provide little evidence that “gender ideology” radicalizes people.

articles.title: A Moment or a Movement? The Effects of Spatial Exposure to the 2017 Women’s March on Political Attitudes and Behavior
articles.abstract: How do social movements affect the public in a polarized era? I examine how the 2017 Women’s March—the largest single-day protest in US history—affected Americans who were exposed to the march in their local communities. I theorize that crowd size moved residents’ political attitudes and behavior in a liberal direction, particularly among Republicans. Using an instrumental variables approach, I find that crowd size increased Republican women’s disapproval of Trump and both Republican women and Republican men’s Democratic vote choice in the 2018 midterm elections. This paper has important implications for understanding the effects of protests that reach a range of communities and focus on identity.

articles.title: Social Cohesion in Iraq: Leveraging Religious, Political, and Tribal Authorities for Conflict Transformation
articles.authors: Mae Anna Chokr, Ali Al-Ahmad, Abbas Aroua
articles.abstract: How can we foster social cohesion by engaging with informal religious and political authorities in conflict contexts, such as present-day Iraq? This report answers this question by outlining a conflict transformation approach developed by Cordoba Peace Institute – Geneva (CPI), and in Samarra, Talafar, and Iraq as a whole, between 2018 and 2023. The methodology used was a combination of: 1) a ‘safe mediation space’ approach and diapraxis, 2) collaboration between insider and outsider mediators, and 3) leveraging formal and informal sources of influence, including religious, political, and tribal. The report aims to learn from the experiences of case studies to guide practitioners applying such methods in other similar contexts.

articles.title: Vanishing Vanguard: Decline of Leadership in Revolutionary Mass Mobilization since the 19th Century
articles.authors: Vadim Ustyuzhanin, Julia Zinkina, Andrey Korotayev
articles.abstract: “Leaderlessness” is widely held to be a defining feature of contemporary mass mobilization, yet the claim rests on a handful of recent cases. We offer the first systematic cross-national analysis of this phenomenon from 1791 to 2019. We show that the absence of leadership is real but older and more modest than claimed: the share of campaigns / revolutions lacking discernible leadership has been rising for two centuries, yet in the 21st century only about a half are leaderless. Testing six explanations drawn from the literature, we find that two factors robustly predict the absence of leadership: student participation and democracy & human-rights goals, that is, “thin” ideology in contrast to “thick” ideologies of the past. We detect no significant effect of coalition breadth, nonviolent tactic, and internet use on leadership. Thus, leaderless mobilization is rooted in who mobilizes and what they demand, but not in scale, tactics, or technology.

articles.title: How Much Labelled Data Is Enough? A Simulation Study of Prompting Strategies for Unbiased and Reliable LLM-Based Annotation Workflows in Social Sciences
articles.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in (computational) social science to annotate text at scale. Typically, this approach requires researchers to provide (enough) gold labels, develop and evaluate candidate prompts, and decide on the most promising prompt. Meanwhile, many questions arise and remain unanswered: How much labelled data is enough? How should prompt evaluation be conducted? In particular, how can researchers prevent overfitting, an important consideration many social scientists are unfamiliar with. To address these questions, this paper reports a simulation study of prompt evaluation workflows for LLM-based text annotation. I compare intentionally biased yet often employed all-data reuse and validation-only baseline strategies with two defensible workflows: a two-way development/evaluation split and a three-way Explore--Select--Evaluate (ESE) workflow. Across 360 simulation scenarios and 360,000 workflow-level simulation results, all-data reuse and validation-only workflows produced positive reporting bias, especially under adaptive prompt development. In contrast, both two-way and ESE workflows had near-zero mean reporting bias and close-to-95% coverage. However, ESE did not generally select stronger prompts. In fixed-candidate settings, two-way selection outperformed ESE because ESE retained less data for formal prompt comparison without gaining any benefit from exploration. In adaptive settings, ESE reduced regret only modestly under some split ratios, while two-way workflows usually selected prompts with higher absolute true performance. The results suggest that a held-out evaluation set is essential, but that a separate Select stage should be used selectively rather than treated as universally optimal.

articles.title: A cautionary tale of industrial decline, economic grievances, and far-right voting
articles.abstract: Economic grievances are central in explaining the rise of right-wing illiberalism. Grievances allow challenger parties to rally around scapegoating outsider groups, such as ethnic minorities, immigrants, or foreigners. Some research argues that continuing decline allows illiberal parties to consolidate power by entrenching and polarizing around such cleavages. However, when illiberal parties are in power and economic decline continues, we argue that, absent cultural cleavages, retrospective economic voting prevails. Zooming in on the case of Trstenik, a Serbian town with a significant industrial legacy, strongly affected by deindustrialization, we leverage data from a novel survey and semi-structured interviews in a mixed-methods approach. We document clear patterns of existing grievances and blame on the government. However, positive, hopeful interpretations also exist among affected individuals. We show that support for the illiberal right-wing incumbent Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) is positively associated with positive interpretations and negatively associated with grievances. Our study contributes an important qualifying account to current debates about the economic roots of right-wing illiberalism by highlighting the importance of scope conditions.

articles.title: Making the Case for an Experiential Approach to Test Validation
articles.abstract: This paper introduces the Experiential Approach to test validation (Araneda, 2023; Araneda & Sireci, 2021), a framework grounded in phenomenology, rhetorical argumentation, and participatory epistemologies. Departing from traditional validation models centered on psychometric inference and technical justification, the Experiential Approach treats the lived experiences of test-takers and stakeholders as primary sources of validity inquiry. Drawing on standpoint theory, situated knowledges, and participatory action research, it reconceptualizes assessment as a system of interrelated devices whose validity depends on how they function in context. The paper contrasts this framework with Kane's argument-based approach, emphasizing its recursive, device-centered structure and its use of normative, functional, comparative, and critical lenses for generating validity claims. It also examines unresolved challenges concerning stakeholder negotiation, face validity, and the political limits of experiential critique. The paper contributes to emerging efforts toward more context-sensitive, pluralistic, and ethically reflexive approaches to validation.

articles.title: Dynamic Democratic Consent: A System Dynamics Framework for Public Trust, Political Communication, and Policy Feedback
articles.abstract: Political communication is often analyzed through event-based models that give lim ited attention to feedback, delay, saturation, and changing public trust. This conceptual paper proposes the Dynamic Democratic Consent framework, integrating selected princi ples from Edward Bernays’ account of public relations with the S-E-E-D behavior modes of Snowball growth, Equilibrium seeking, Elastic adjustment, and feedback-loop Dominance. The framework extends the conventional resource categories of manpower, mindpower, and money by treating algorithmic media infrastructure as a conditional fourth dimension. It maps an eight-stage communication-planning process onto reinforcing and balancing feed back structures, perception delays, demographic capacity, and institutional trust. Simulated reference modes illustrate how political-support momentum may encounter electoral satura tion, how delayed perception and corrective response may produce oscillatory adjustment, and how divergence between communication and policy delivery may weaken institutional trust and contract effective support capacity. A four-stage diagnostic process is proposed for describing trajectories, identifying feedback structures, designing policy interventions, and examining potential behavioral shifts. The framework is exploratory rather than predictive. Empirical estimation, comparative case testing, sensitivity analysis, and ethical evaluation are required before it can support applied political analysis.

articles.title: Seizing the Agenda: Polarization and Legislative Autonomy in Brazilian Presidentialism
articles.authors: Jamil Civitarese, Fabiano Guilherme Mendes Santos
articles.abstract: Brazilian coalitional presidentialism has long been read as a system in which the executive sets the agenda and the legislature holds a veto. We argue that, since the mid-2010s, the Congress has been building agenda-setting power. We account for the shift with a formal spatial framework in which a legislature weighs the cost of acquiring agenda power against the costs caused by the executive it expects to face. Two forces drive the investment: the rightward movement of a median legislator dissatisfied with the status quo and the recent polarization of the Executive, a partner that became too radical and costly to legislate with. Reading the record from Lula's first governments through Lula III, we show how the realignment of agenda power came to constrain the president who now has to both manage the coalition and to accommodate increasing policy demands from the legislature.

articles.title: Towards a Typology of Islamic Higher Education in Europe: A Comparative Analysis of Institutional Models
articles.abstract: This article examines the emergence and institutional diversity of Islamic higher education in Europe and develops a comparative typology of its principal institutional models. While existing scholarship has focused primarily on individual countries, institutions, or debates concerning imam training, a systematic comparative framework for understanding the broader landscape of Islamic higher education remains underdeveloped. Using a comparative institutional analysis of developments in the Netherlands, Germany, Belgium, Austria, England, France, Spain, and Italy, the study examines historical trajectories, state–religion relations, institutional structures, accreditation systems, leadership formation, and sources of legitimacy. The findings demonstrate that Islamic higher education in Europe has not developed through a single institutional pathway. Instead, five ideal-type models can be identified: the Independent Islamic University Model, the State-Integrated Islamic Theology Model, the Seminary-Based Model, the Hybrid Partnership Model, and the Emerging and Transitional Model. The study contributes to the literature by providing a comparative framework for analyzing institutional diversity and by proposing a typology that facilitates future research on Islamic higher education, Muslim institutionalization, and religious leadership in Europe.

articles.title: Between Disintermediation and Inertia: Preprints and the Digital Transformation of the Scientific Knowledge Order
articles.abstract: Informed by work on the digital transformation of traditional knowledge orders, this study examines how researchers use preprints relative to journal publication, and how they perceive preprints’ credibility, benefits, and risks. Evidence comes from a cross-disciplinary survey of 1,403 researchers affiliated with German universities who had previously served as corresponding authors on Web of Science-indexed publications. Corresponding authors indexed in Web of Science are not representative of the scientific community as a whole, and participation was low relative to the number invited, so the estimates describe the respondent sample rather than population prevalence. Unlike studies that recruit through preprint servers, however, this frame also reaches researchers who have never posted a preprint. We investigate five dimensions: (1) adoption rates and disciplinary variations, (2) publication practices, (3) audience orientation and reported feedback, (4) motivations for preprint use, and (5) scientific perceptions of preprints’ implications for research integrity and credibility. Our findings reveal disciplinary differences: 48.6% of natural scientists had uploaded a preprint compared with 18.6% of humanities scholars. Among adopters, reported motivations emphasized access, open science, and speed. Respondents also expressed concerns about credibility and premature public reporting. Intended audiences and reported feedback were concentrated within the scientific community, with little frequent feedback reported from journalists, policymakers, industry, or citizens. Most users posted preprints alongside the journal publication process, although 21.6% included having no intention to publish elsewhere among the circumstances in which they usually posted. These findings describe preprints as a widely used but unevenly adopted publication mode that commonly coexists with formal peer review, with implications for scientific policy and research integrity.

articles.title: From science to policy: A multilevel framework for measuring institutional policy engagement through Overton
articles.authors: Daniel Torres-Salinas, Wenceslao Arroyo-Machado, Nicolas Robinson-Garcia, Esteban Romero-Frías
articles.abstract: This study presents a multilevel framework to assess the policy attention of academic institutions using Overton as a primary data source. We illustrate this framework through a case study of the University of Granada, combining Overton policy mentions, OpenAlex topics, and bibliometric analysis. Results show policy engagement particularly concentrated in health, physical, and social sciences, with mentions from key governmental and intergovernmental organisations. The study quantifies the university's visibility in policy documents, classifies mentions by scientific domain and issuer type, maps 1,145 research topics to Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), and identifies seven researchers whose work aligns with Spain's Urban Agenda. The findings demonstrate the value of Overton for mapping the presence of institutional research in policy documents and tracing science-policy linkages. However, given the well-documented risks of misuse of bibliometric indicators in research evaluation, users of this framework should be aware of key interpretive boundaries: policy mentions should not be equated with policy impact; raw mention counts cannot establish reliable temporal trends given Overton's continuous expansion; and geographic and linguistic distributions of mentions reflect Overton's structural indexing biases toward OECD countries rather than real-world policy engagement. With these caveats, the framework offers a scalable model for institutional policy engagement assessment.

articles.title: Mapping film commissions in Brazil: Intermediary organizations and institutionalization dynamics in challenging creative ecosystems
articles.abstract: This article presents a panorama of film commissions in Brazil, describing their diverse intermediary roles, tracing their distinct institutionalization paths and reflecting on how trends toward institutional isomorphism or divergence unfold in this emerging field within the Brazilian cultural and creative industries (CCIs). Based on qualitative interviews with 15 film commission representatives, it reveals that these organizations act as strategic intermediaries within local audiovisual ecosystems and follow diverse institutionalization trajectories, with some operating independently with minimal resources and others benefitting from more robust budgets and institutional structures. As relatively new players navigating the uncertainties of Brazil’s cultural and creative landscape, film commissions exhibit a degree of isomorphism in following similar institutional templates, performing analogous logistical functions, and exchanging best practices in consultancies and sector events. Yet, divergence also occurs, particularly due to local and regional inequalities in cultural funding and industry development, which fundamentally shape how each of them operates. Despite their increasing prominence in creative ecosystems worldwide, film commissions remain under-researched, particularly in the Global South. This study fills in this gap by examining the case of Brazil and offering a more nuanced understanding of cultural intermediation and the dynamics of institutional homogeneity and diversity, especially in contexts characterized by significant local and regional variation in the development, size, and funding of the CCIs.

articles.title: Digital Transformation and Strategic Adaptation in Small Businesses: Evidence from Local Interview Case Studies
articles.authors: Pranay Saripalli, Shaurya Yadav, Ayush Tripathi
articles.abstract: This qualitative case study examines how small businesses adapt to digital innovation, financial constraints, and external economic pressures. The study draws on structured in-person interviews with owners and representatives of three local businesses—Empxre, Bam Clothing, and American Hide—to examine how business owners assess the costs and benefits of digital adoption and sustain competitiveness amid changing market conditions. Existing research has established that small and medium-sized enterprise (SME) digitalization can improve business performance and customer engagement, but less attention has been given to the strategic reasoning that shapes individual firms’ adaptation decisions. The findings highlight the importance of aligning digital transformation with broader business strategy, customer needs, and available financial resources. Empxre demonstrates how an omnichannel approach incorporating websites and social media can support customer engagement.
