articles.title: Imagining transformative pathways towards peaceful and equitable futures in the Korean peninsula
articles.authors: HyeJin Kim, Vitnia Lee, Hyeonjeong Kim, Miyoung Yeo, Yeoungjun Yeo, Youngcheol Cho, Gwanwoo Jin, Justin Johnson, Bohun Kang, Dirk N. Karger
articles.abstract: The Korean Peninsula faces the intertwined challenges of a polycrisis: an unresolved war and rapid development followed by demographic contraction, inequality, accelerating biodiversity loss, and intensifying climate risk. Achieving nature- and people-positive futures in this context requires finding alternative pathways: levers and actors of change, and their sequences and scaling. Citizens constructed transformative pathways from present-day Korea to four Korean Nature Futures visions. A methodology combined the Nature Futures Framework, Imagination Infrastructure, and Seeds of Good Anthropocene with narratives refined through the multi-level perspective and social-ecological systems theory. The four 2025-2050 pathways trace changes through five phases: present-day challenges, seeds of change, breaking points and shocks, and the emergence and stabilisation of new systems by 2050. Comparative analysis across ten domains – social, technological, ecological, economic, political, cultural, military, religious, identity, and the DMZ – identifies shared strategies and pathway-specific mechanisms. Across pathways, the DMZ is reimagined from a line of division into an anchor of ecological peace, with human and non-human actors recognised as agents of transformation. The study offers a transferable methodology for transformative scenario development in contested geopolitical settings and a proof of concept for anticipatory governance toward equitable and peaceful futures ‘Living in Harmony with Nature’.

articles.title: Gambling Industry Political Engagement, 2020–2026: A Proof-of-Concept for Auditing of Political Transparency Data using a GPT-assisted Pipeline.

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: Background: Commercial political activity is increasingly recognised within the broader framework of commercial determinants of health. However, UK gambling-related political engagement is fragmented across separate transparency systems. This study examined whether a GPT-assisted, independently reconciled workflow could integrate these records and provide a more complete picture of disclosed political activity. Methods: A retrospective analysis was conducted of UK gambling-related political engagement from 1 January 2020 to 25 August 2026 across three streams: (1) Electoral Commission political donations; (2) MPs’ declared hospitality/gifts and funded visits; and (3) ministerial meetings within the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport / Department for Culture, Media and Sport (DCMS). GPT was used to retrieve, structure, link and classify records against a reference frame of gambling organisations, which was derived from multiple public sources, including Gambling Commission registers, Companies House records, company and trade-body information, and historical ownership and corporate-relationship evidence. After classification, each of the three streams underwent an independent GPT reconciliation pass, followed by bounded human adjudication of unresolved cases. A final audit compared the final donations and hospitality datasets with previous UK journalism and civil-society reporting. Results: The principal analysis identified 127 donations with confirmed active commercial gambling connections, worth £7.73 million, from donors with a confirmed material commercial gambling connection active on the donation date. Of this value, 85.4% went to the Conservative political family and 13.0% to Reform UK. MPs declared 176 qualifying hospitality/gift events involving 71 MPs, worth £236,162, plus four funded visits. The ministerial-meeting census contained 272 gambling-related events, of which 86 involved principal commercial-industry actors. Across the 138-group company universe, meeting frequency was positively associated with both donation frequency (Spearman ρ=.390; p=.00004) and hospitality frequency (ρ=.487; p=.00001), although these associations are observational and non-causal. In the final audit against previously reported figures, 291 of the observed donation/hospitality records had no apparent or obvious match in the prior-reporting examined; and one genuine omission in this analysis was identified and corrected (related to hospitality). Conclusions: Systematic linkage across transparency systems revealed a scale and pattern of gambling-connected political activity that is not apparent from individual registers or prior headline reporting. GPT made this integration tractable, but independent reconciliation and human adjudication were essential. Integrated monitoring of political activity may therefore be important for understanding the commercial determinants of health in gambling and other harmful commodity industries.

articles.title: A Fork in the Road for Global AI Governance: To Repair or Reconfigure Expert-Led Governance?

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has become a live object of global governance, with expert-led institutional arrangements emerging across an international regime complex. While scholarship on epistemic communities and science-policy interfaces treats expertise as a mechanism for coordination under uncertainty, recent work in Objectual International Relations (O-IR) and Science and Technology Studies foregrounds knowledge politics, contested authority, and the co-productive character of governance. We bring these perspectives into conversation with AI governance through a reflexive workshop design using Nominal Group Technique, drawing on two expert workshops in the UK and US. Findings show that expert panels remain valued for structuring debate, coordinating knowledge, and lending legitimacy to policy action. Yet participants identified tensions around exclusion, elite and private capture, weak accountability, geopolitical constraints, and temporal misalignment between institutional processes and technological change. An object-centered analysis further shows that AI remains an unstable governance object; the knowledge required to govern it is contested and unevenly distributed; and expertise itself is politically charged and institutionally unsettled. We synthesize these tensions into two pathways: Repair and Reconfiguration. Repair seeks to stabilize AI as a governable object, standardize relevant knowledge, and secure expert authority through institutional continuity and procedural refinement. Reconfiguration seeks to keep AI contested, broaden credible forms of knowledge, and reshape expertise through participation, reflexivity, and engagement with politics. The framework provides a critical lens for assessing emerging institutional designs for global AI governance and the trade-offs they entail.

articles.title: Different histories, similar discrimination: Field experimental evidence of discrimination against Black parents in the Dutch childcare market
articles.authors: Stefanie Sprong, Valentina Di Stasio, Bram Lancee, Eva Zschirnt
articles.abstract: While a vast body of research documents discrimination against ethnoracial minorities, including Black people, existing studies rarely consider how the diverse historical relationships of different Black groups may shape patterns of discrimination. Using data from the first field experiment in the Dutch childcare sector (N = 1,354), we examine discrimination against ascribed Black parents enquiring about childcare spots in the Netherlands. Rather than aggregating all ascribed Black parents into a single category, we compare ascribed Black parents with names associated with former Dutch colonies to those with names associated with Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA), expecting the former group to face less discrimination. We find robust evidence that ascribed Black parents face discrimination in access to childcare: compared to ascribed White majority parents, they are significantly less likely to receive a spot offer, and their enquiries are more likely to be ignored altogether. SSA ascribed Black parents are also more likely to experience neglectful treatment in written correspondence. Otherwise, levels of discrimination do not significantly differ between former-colonies and SSA ascribed Black parents, suggesting discrimination against Black parents more generally.

articles.title: Dynamics of Self-Employment Following Motherhood: A Comparison Between Korea and the United States
articles.abstract: Parenthood increases the need to adjust paid work, especially for mothers, who continue to shoulder a disproportionate share of carework. This makes it important to understand not only whether mothers remain employed after childbirth, but also how they reorganize work across the life course. This paper examines self-employment as one potential way mothers incorporate flexibility into their post-birth careers. Adopting a life course perspective, I compare new mothers in South Korea and the United States and trace their employment arrangements from first birth to ten years afterward. Using descriptive analysis, sequence analysis, and multinomial logistic regression, I assess whether self-employment emerges as a distinct pathway in mothers’ careers and how its role differs across institutional contexts. The results first show that self-employment is more common in mothers’ careers than cross-sectional estimates would suggest in both countries. However, the way it is incorporated differs substantially. In Korea, self-employment more often follows spells of non-work and is more likely to be full-time, suggesting that it can operate as part of a return to paid work strategy when rse-entry into wage employment is difficult. In the United States, self-employment is more often part-time and embedded within continued attachment to wage employment. Multinomial logistic regression provides only limited support for the idea that self-employment trajectories primarily function as a flexibility strategy, as they are only weakly associated with women’s educational resources and are not clearly associated with second birth. Overall, the findings show that self-employment is part of many mothers’ post-birth careers, but not a general flexibility strategy; its meaning is shaped by institutional context.

articles.title: Dimensions of Division: Structuring Ideological Polarization During Poland’s Democratic Backsliding
articles.authors: Marta Kołczyńska, Maciej Sychowiec, Oliwia Szczupska
articles.abstract: Research on democratic backsliding increasingly views mass polarization as a mechanism that facilitates democratic erosion. This study examines trajectories of ideological polarization in Poland between 1997 and 2023, a period encompassing democratic backsliding whose onset is typically dated to 2015. Using repeated issue-based questions from the Polish National Election Study (POLNES), we distinguish three aspects of polarization: radicalization of individuals’ positions on single issues, issue alignment (system-level correlation of issue positions across different domains), and issue partisanship (the extent to which issue positions are explained by party preferences). We find no evidence of increased single-issue radicalization over the studied period. By contrast, both issue alignment and issue partisanship increased, particularly on socio-cultural issues, with little change on economic issues. These trends are not linear: they emerge around the 2011 election and persist thereafter. This pattern is consistent with theories that view changes in mass polarization as facilitating conditions for democratic backsliding. Additionally, our findings highlight the heterogeneous nature of polarization and show that focusing on single issues or unidimensional ideological scales can obscure important changes in the structure of mass belief systems.

articles.title: Sustainable Urban River Space Transformations: An Interdisciplinary Spatial Agenda for Research and Practice
articles.authors: Claudiu Forgaci, Francesco Nattino, Angelica Stan, Fakhereh Alidoost, Mila Avellar Montezuma, Bilge Nur Bektaş, Lieke de Boer, Daniele Cannatella, Rodrigo d'Avila, Ilse Ellenbroek

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: Riverfront regeneration increasingly features in current sustainable urban transformations worldwide. However, this phenomenon is not yet grasped in its full complexity, which challenges our understanding of what constitutes a sustainable transformation. In this paper, we argue that adopting a morphological approach that treats rivers and cities equally is essential for understanding urban river spaces and their transformations. Drawing on 17 worldwide cases of river space transformation, we identify recurring challenges and opportunities, including climate adaptation, land-use change, data availability, context sensitivity, and knowledge transfer. We inventory current methods, datasets, and tools to assess their suitability and sufficiency for answering current research questions and enabling new ones. We also posit that integrated and scalable approaches are needed to combine qualitative and quantitative methods, support cross-case comparison, and remain adaptable to local conditions. As a first foundational step towards local integrated and global cross-case analyses, we introduce urban river space delineation as the basis for comparable analysis and present rcrisp, an open-source tool for automated and scalable morphological delineation of urban river spaces. Finally, we emphasise that advancing this agenda requires community and capacity building across disciplines and sectors, so that methods and tools can be shared, refined and extended. By connecting cases, methods and communities, the paper calls for collective action to build a common language and evidence base for sustainable urban river space transformation.

articles.title: Adaptive Solutions: An interdisciplinary Study of Human and Organizational Adaptation during the Covid-19 Pandemic.
articles.abstract: This exploratory qualitative study examines how professionals and organizational leaders connected to the Brazilian pharmaceutical and healthcare sectors experienced and responded to adaptive challenges arising from organizational disruption during the COVID-19 pandemic. The study adopts an interdisciplinary perspective at the intersection of Business, Organizational Psychology, and Organizational Studies, conceptualizing adaptation as a process involving both organizational responses and changes in human behavior, relationships, expectations, and established ways of working. The study combines a focused literature review with six semi-structured interviews conducted between July and September 2022 with professionals working across pharmaceutical/medical affairs, commercial operations, human resources, marketing and sales, information technology, and Agile transformation. The analysis was organized around five interconnected domains: leadership, Agile management, Agile HR management, performance management, and knowledge management. Particular attention was given to the distinction between technical challenges, which can be addressed through existing expertise and established procedures, and adaptive challenges, which may require changes in behaviors, assumptions, relationships, and patterns of interaction. The findings indicate that organizational disruption exposed limitations that could not always be addressed through technological or procedural interventions alone. Participants described changes in work structures, stakeholder relationships, leadership practices, collaboration, prioritization, communication, and employee support. Agile practices were described as one mechanism for enabling shorter learning cycles, greater collaboration, distributed decision-making, and adaptation to changing stakeholder needs. At the same time, the interviews suggest that Agile practices were more meaningful when accompanied by attention to people, relationships, communication, leadership, and the capacity to reconsider established ways of working. The study contributes to interdisciplinary research on human and organizational adaptation by connecting external disruption with individual and collective responses within organizational settings. Rather than presenting Agile management as an independent solution, the findings suggest that adaptive capacity emerges through the interaction of human behavior, leadership, organizational practices, knowledge processes, and changing environmental demands. The study offers exploratory implications for organizational psychology, organizational behavior, leadership, human resource management, and organizational change research. Keywords: human adaptation; organizational adaptation; adaptive challenges; organizational change; organizational psychology; leadership; Agile management; knowledge work; pharmaceutical industry; COVID-19.

articles.title: Responsible AI Risk Governance in Public Service Organizations—Insights from a Meta-Synthesis
articles.authors: Kristina S. Weißmüller, Menno J. Hoppen, Gjalt De Graaf

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: The use of AI in public service provision can reshape citizen-state interactions, introducing new risks and challenges to ensure safe, inclusive, and just applications that do not discriminate against vulnerable citizens. This study examines how public service organizations govern these risks. Drawing on a meta-synthesis of AI risk governance scholarship (n=56), we synthesize the empirical evidence from a value-based risk governance perspective. We identify four governance challenges: (1) establishing substantive pre-assessment before adoption; (2) enabling informed, plural, and revisable appraisal; (3) ensuring meaningful human oversight during implementation; and (4) preserving organizational ownership in ensuring that monitoring and feedback are connected to correction and learning. For each challenge, the synthesis identifies failure patterns and proposes solutions on how to avoid them. Integrating these findings, we develop a novel evidence-based AI risk governance framework for public organizations. Advancing the discourse on technology risk governance and administrative burden in the age of AI, this study provides an organizational explanation for AI risk governance success and failure, offering insights for theory and practice.

articles.title: After CAHOOTS: Service decline, shifting police attention, and a rising arrest rate
articles.authors: Nathan Burton, Mathilde Lafay, Leo Uhlig, Alex Gollier, Jennifer Linnaea, Chris Medina, Rori Rohlfs
articles.abstract: For more than three decades, CAHOOTS dispatched unarmed teams of medics and crisis workers to certain 911 calls in Eugene, Oregon. On April 7, 2025, the program ceased operations in Eugene, though it continues in neighboring Springfield. This report provides a quantitative analysis of 911 calls and responses in the aftermath of the closure, attempting to account for the roughly 235 calls per week that CAHOOTS had been handling. We find that police now spend substantially more time on CAHOOTS-type call categories, even though the Eugene Police Department (EPD) has absorbed only a minority of CAHOOTS’ former call volume. More than half of the former demand no longer appears in any city record available to us, and the calls that do still receive a response end in arrest roughly twice as often.

articles.title: Weathering the Crisis: How American Insurers Planned for Climate Change, 2012-2023
articles.abstract: How did the American insurance industry respond to the growing threat of climate change? We show that insurers were confident in their ability to quantify increased climate risks and either raise rates or exit risky geographies and thus maintain profitability. This strategy was plausible given the short term of property insurance contracts: homeowners might have 30-year mortgages, but home insurance contracts are typically one year. At the same time, insurers continued to underwrite and invest in fossil fuel companies and engaged very little with climate policy. This analysis extends prior research on the “tragedy of the horizon” in the relationship between finance and climate change and contrasts with predictions that insurers should be natural supporters of climate change policy.

articles.title: Officials Hedge, Public Doubts: The Certainty Gap in China's AI-Education Discourse (2020–2026)

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: Chinese universities have launched a wave of “AI+X” programs that train students in professional domains—architecture, journalism, accounting, teaching—to use generative AI tools, often before any consensus exists that AI-assisted learning improves educational outcomes. Empirical research to date finds no reliable improvement in grades, documents cognitive offloading, and leaves long-term learning effects unmeasured. This paper asks whether that disconnect between institutional acceleration and empirical uncertainty surfaces in discourse: do official and public articulations of AI’s role in education differ in epistemic certainty, and is any such gap innate or emergent? We construct two corpora spanning 2020–2026—official discourse (policy documents and official-media posts, n = 691) and public discourse (Weibo, n = 11,345)—and measure four dimensions of epistemic stance (certainty markers, presupposition, hedging, and tolerance of uncertainty) using a hybrid design that pairs a transparent dictionary with LLM zero-shot coding, cross-validated at a mean Cohen's κ of .926. Three findings stand out. First, before ChatGPT the two corpora were epistemically indistinguishable, replicating Zeng, Chan, and Schäfer’s (2020) “striking similarity”; the gap emerged only after 2023. Second, the gap is not unidirectional: official discourse presupposes AI’s value more (D2 = 82.8% vs. 77.2%; policy documents 90.7%) yet hedges and acknowledges uncertainty significantly more than the public does (D3 and D4 reversed)—a pattern we term institutional hedging. Third, public epistemic stance is bimodal (absolute assertion or absolute doubt), whereas official discourse is layered across premise and expression. Time-series and difference-in-differences analyses locate two shocks—ChatGPT (2023) broke the stance layer (public D2 fell from 82% to 52%), and DeepSeek-R1 (2025) deepened the expression layer (D3 reached its series maximum)—suggesting the public underwent an epistemic learning process, first learning to doubt and then to qualify. We contribute a measurable, multidimensional discourse variable for the certainty gap and a hybrid coding template for large-scale epistemic-stance annotation.

articles.title: Partisan disparities in the production and uptake of science
articles.authors: Alexander Furnas, Jian Gao, Yian Yin, Dashun Wang

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: Scientific institutions are designed to produce and evaluate claims through shared evidentiary and disciplinary standards, yet they are embedded in an increasingly polarized society. This fundamental tension raises the question of whether scientists’ partisan alignment is associated with the production, circulation, and uptake of scientific knowledge. Here we integrate campaign-finance records, faculty rosters, voter-registration data, an original survey of approximately 7,000 active U.S. scientists, bibliometric data, and measures of uptake in policy documents, patents, and news coverage to map the partisan composition of the scientific workforce, the knowledge it produces, and its uptake within and beyond science. We find that U.S. science is politically asymmetric without being ideologically homogeneous: scientists who make political contributions are overwhelmingly Democratic-aligned, and this asymmetry has widened over time, yet the broader workforce includes many Independents and substantial ideological heterogeneity within partisan groups. Among scientists with strong, behaviorally observed partisan alignments, Democratic- and Republican-authored papers are systematically distinguishable in semantic content across all fields, even after conditioning on fine-grained topic and year. Differences in total scientific citation rates are modest and have narrowed over time, whereas citations occur more often within the same partisan author communities than expected under topic- and year-preserving null models. Uptake beyond science also varies by partisan authorship and domain, with the clearest directional selectivity among ideological think tanks. These findings reveal an uneven profile of partisan association across U.S. science, visible in published content and directional attention, but comparatively limited in aggregate scientific recognition. This profile is consistent with a scientific system in which shared evaluative standards coexist with political structure in the production and circulation of knowledge, with implications for science’s capacity to remain a common evidentiary resource in a polarized society.

articles.title: Where Can Older Workers Go? Regional Restructuring and Occupational Opportunity
articles.abstract: This paper examines how occupational restructuring within local labour markets shapes the employment opportunities of older workers. Using longitudinal Swedish register data covering workers across 69 functional local labour markets between 2017 and 2023, we show that greater occupational restructuring is associated with greater occupational narrowing among older workers. This relationship is moderated by local labour market characteristics. Thicker and more dynamic labour markets, with greater occupational diversity and job churning, provide broader opportunities for occupational adjustment. The findings highlight the importance of regional opportunity structures for old-age employment in ageing economies.

articles.title: Formal and Informal Institutions Interactively Increase Judicial Independence: Evidence from Israel and Cross-National Data
articles.abstract: Comparative research emphasizes that independent judiciaries act as bulwarks against democratic backsliding. Yet we know less about why judicial independence is more resilient in some cases than others. Whereas existing scholarship often contrasts the effects of formal versus informal institutions, this paper emphasizes how their interaction fosters judicial independence. I theorize that one understudied institution—a super-majority requirement for selecting high court judges—increases judicial independence. Moreover, this formal institution better protects judicial independence when complemented by an informal institution—a practice of appointing groups of ideologically distinct judges that I call the Noah’s Ark strategy. I test this institutional theory using cross-national and within-country evidence. Leveraging original data on judicial selection institutions in 139 countries, I find super-majority requirements are significantly associated with increased judicial independence. To show how formal and informal institutions interact, I conduct a case study of the country with the world’s highest super-majority requirement, Israel. Using quantitative data on 16,000 Israeli Supreme Court decisions and qualitative interviews with high-ranking judges and politicians, I show that formal and informal institutions constrained the government’s judicial appointments—but that the government’s undermining of informal institutions weakened judicial independence. These findings illuminate how the interaction of formal and informal institutions fosters judicial independence and democratic resilience.

articles.title: The Rise of Competitive Authoritarianism in Israel: The Paradox of Uneven and Contested Competitive Authoritarianism
articles.abstract: Scholars and democracy indices disagree over whether prominent cases of autocratization have crossed the threshold into competitive authoritarianism. One reason for these disagreements, we argue, is that there are varieties of competitive authoritarianism. We theorize that competitive authoritarian regimes vary in the degree to which they are uneven, repressive, and contested. We then evaluate empirically whether Israel meets Levitsky and Way’s definition of competitive authoritarianism. We find that by Levitsky and Way’s criteria, Israel crossed the line into competitive authoritarianism under Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. But competitive authoritarianism is not a one-size-fits-all category. We show that Israel’s competitive authoritarian regime is uneven, in that autocratization is more severe in some areas than others; less repressive than many autocracies; and contested, in that opposition parties remain competitive, even when they are structurally disadvantaged. This unevenness and contestedness have led to Israel’s misclassification thus far.

articles.title: Book Review Multimodality and Time: A Social Semiotic Approach (preprint)
articles.abstract: This review examines Theo van Leeuwen's Multimodality and Time: A Social Semiotic Approach (2025), which foregrounds the role of timing and rhythm in meaning-making. The book develops a Social Semiotic approach for analysing time-based multimodal texts and performances, including music, film, language, and everyday interactions. Distinguishing between time, timing, social timing, and time-based texts, van Leeuwen argues that timing is socially constructed and that rhythmic structuring is central to how meaning unfolds across modes. The review considers the book's treatment of rhythm, temporality, and multimodal analysis, and discusses the ways in which it extends existing multimodal approaches by bringing temporality to the forefront of analysis. The review concludes that the book makes a significant contribution to Multimodal Social Semiotics and visual communication research and offers valuable directions for future research.

articles.title: What Survives Multilingual Competition? Ecology-Dependent Selection in World Englishes and Heritage Grammars
articles.abstract: World Englishes and heritage languages both develop under multilingual conditions. One is usually studied through community-level contact-variety stabilization, the other through individual bilingual restructuring. It remains unclear whether the same feature-level pressures predict outcomes across these two ecologies. This exploratory study tests a simple selection model in which perceptual salience, contextual frequency, form–meaning transparency, cross-linguistic congruence, and regularity are expected to favor the survival or expansion of a variant. A manually audited pilot dataset contains 24 world English/contact outcomes and 21 heritage-language outcomes. Contact outcomes are coded from eWAVE; heritage outcomes are traced to primary experimental or corpus studies. Ordered-logit models provide no robust evidence for a general salience advantage. The results suggest that a shared feature-pool selection framework of multilingual restructuring may be conditioned by ecology. For world Englishes, the findings point to a stabilization logic in which recoverability, structural support, source availability, and repeated community use can outweigh raw perceptual prominence.

articles.title: To adopt or not to adopt? Moving beyond a binary conceptualization of farmer’s adoption decisions
articles.authors: Emma Chris Luka Windey, Tina Venema, Agnes van den Pol-van Dasselaar, Hens Runhaar
articles.abstract: Sustainable Farming literature often frames adoption as a binary choice, overlooking decision-making complexity. Drawing on innovation studies, this paper introduces a framework for analyzing adoption decision processes. We examined two types of species-rich grasslands (SRG) as case studies, covering the following decision stages: persuasion, decision, rejection, implementation, confirmation, and discontinuation. We conducted a survey among Dutch dairy farmers (n = 91) and assessed their current decision stage, drivers and barriers to SRG adoption, and farm characteristics. Results indicated that farm characteristics differed across decision stages in nature conservation collective membership for extensive-SRG (E-SRG), but did not differ significantly far any other characteristics for E-SRG, or for any characteristics in the adoption of productive-SRG (P-SRG). For E-SRG, significant differences emerged across stages for several drivers, but not barriers; rejectors stood out most distinctly. For P-SRG, both drivers and barriers varied significantly across stages. Drivers differed most between rejectors and recent implementers, while the confirmation stage was most distinct for barriers. These findings advance theory by showing the value of distinguishing decision stages in the adoption process. Practically, identifying farmer’ current decision stage can guide more efficient policy mixes, enabling targeted interventions that calibrate policy effort to actual needs.

articles.title: Anonymity In Contemporary Political Discourse: Implications of Citizenship And State
articles.abstract: This paper makes an attempt in bringing anonymity into contemporary political discourse as the issue is getting entangled in political debates more and more which is situated in the debate on anonymity that went on in the house of commons of UK parliament. Hitherto the state has enjoyed the monopoly over space but this paper suggests the rise of the internet and decentralised system databases creates cyberspace which defies the monopoly of state power. Further, it explores the implications for the state, citizenship and anonymity.

articles.title: Who cares? The gendered nature of mobility of care in São Paulo
articles.authors: Joana Barros, Agnes Silva de Araujo

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: Quantitative evidence on mobility of care remains scarce and geographically uneven because conventional surveys classify trips by destination and purpose, obscuring caring responsibilities within the evidence used for transport planning. This study expands evidence from the Global South by examining the prevalence, characteristics and gendered distribution of mobility of care in the São Paulo Metropolitan Region. Carrying-passenger trips from the 2023 Origin–Destination Survey are used as a partial proxy for mobility of care and combined with trip-purpose information to distinguish caring activities. Descriptive and negative binomial analyses examine differences by gender, age, race and socioeconomic stratum and interactions between gender and these characteristics, including household car ownership. Carrying passengers accounted for 15.6% of adult trips and displayed distinctive patterns of purpose, mode and trip frequency. Women recorded higher rates than men, particularly for school- and home-related trips, whereas men’s carrying was relatively more work-related. Gender gaps differed in magnitude by race and in both magnitude and direction across the life course. Rather than following a progressive socioeconomic gradient, gender disparities formed a nonlinear U-shape, narrowing to apparent parity in the middle strata but widening asymmetrically at both ends. Car ownership further differentiated gender gaps by socioeconomic stratum and trip purpose. Methodologically, the findings support carrying-passenger data as a useful, although incomplete, means of making care visible in conventional travel surveys. Conceptually, they challenge uniform and gender-neutral accounts of everyday mobility, demonstrating that inequalities in mobility of care emerge through intersections between social positions, caring purposes and household transport resources.

articles.title: Urban veg*ns and rural grillmasters? Local context has a moderate effect on meat consumption
articles.abstract: This paper deepens the role of what we call ‘local geographies of meat consumption’. The countryside is stereotypically portrayed as a conservative bastion with traditional, meat-centric meals on the table, while urban centres are viewed as progressive hotspots for vegetarians and vegans (veg*ns). Drawing on georeferenced survey data, we demonstrate with a multilevel regression analysis how local community is associated with meat-related diets in the Netherlands. This paper shows the relevance of going beyond the conventional urban-rural constellation, by incorporating a broader and more varied set of local context factors, including political culture, agriculture and food environment. In doing so, we account for individual characteristics such as gender, age, education, and political attitudes. The results show that there are local context effects, albeit to a modest degree. Individual characteristics, most prominently gender, are more strongly associated with veg*n diets. Nevertheless, independent of individual background, people living in highly progressive communities are more likely to follow a flexitarian diet, while those in areas with strong populist radical right support or intensive animal agriculture are more likely to be meat eaters. Our results suggest that the political and agricultural context of local community significantly influences the choice for meat-related diets, rather than urban-rural settings alone.

articles.title: Housework, Childcare, Organizing, Waiting, and Employment: Parents' Time Use Patterns by Number of Children
articles.abstract: Objective: This study examines how family size shapes parents’ daily timescapes. Background: Research on family size often treats number of children as a linear control and focuses on time spent in core childcare and housework tasks, limiting understanding of time pressures, including “support work” in larger families. Method: Using the American Time Use Survey (ATUS; 2005–2024), we compare time use by family size and gender across: (1) physical and interactive childcare; (2) childcare-related services, organizing, waiting, and attending; (3) housework and purchasing; (4) household travel; and (5) employment. Tempograms describe daily patterns, and OLS regression estimates associations between family size and time use, adjusting for demographic differences. Results: After adjustment, mothers’ time in physical and interactive childcare does not increase with second or third children. Instead, each additional child increases time in household labor that supports children – housework and purchasing, household travel, and childcare-related organizing, waiting, and attending - and reduces employment time. For fathers, additional children show little association with either household labor or employment. Conclusion: Larger families substantially reshape mothers’ timescapes while leaving fathers’ time largely consistent and centered on employment. Implications: Focusing only on core childcare and housework tasks understates the impact of additional children. Accounting for time-bound “support work” is essential to understanding mothers’ patterns of household and paid labor, especially with the addition of subsequent children.

articles.title: NATO’s Strategic Culture(s). Public Opinion on Arms Transfers in Top Five Exporting Countries
articles.authors: Fabian Haggerty, Lukas Rudolph, Paul Thurner
articles.abstract: Weapons transfers to foreign countries - a proliferation of conventional coercive technologies - became politicized in Western democracies in recent years, whereby fundamental tradeoffs between security-related, economic, and normative aspects are discussed. We propose that how these tradeoffs are solved is indicative of a more general strategic culture of countries. We investigate how the public views these tradeoffs and how homogeneous the underlying preference structure in NATO's top arms-exporting democracies (the US, UK, France, Germany, and Italy) is. Using a multidimensional measurement strategy via a conjoint experiment (N~10,000), we show that normative aspects predominate for all populations when forming preferences on export policies. However, we observe that Germany and Italy are essentially divided from the other three countries, regarding whether security aspects are considered in preference formation. Building on recent (machine learning) methods, we propose that this difference can be primarily attributed to the country of the respondents, indicating different strategic subcultures.

articles.title: Valid and Reliable? Basic and Expanded Recommendations for Psychometric Reporting and Quality Assessment
articles.authors: Magnus Johansson, Marit Preuter, Jeanette Melin
articles.abstract: Improving the validity, reliability, and replicability of research in the social and health sciences depends on the quality of measurement. We argue that judging whether the sum score of a multi-item measure adequately represents the intended latent variable rests on four basic criteria — unidimensionality, local independence of items, ordered response categories, and invariance — which can serve as a minimal checklist for end users assessing the quality of a psychometric study. A central recommendation is to stop interpreting model and item fit against rule-of-thumb critical values and instead use simulation-based cutoffs tailored to the data at hand. Because most published psychometric work relies on rule-of-thumb cutoffs, established scales are in urgent need of re-analysis with appropriate methods. We provide an up-to-date overview of methods for evaluating each criterion within Rasch Measurement Theory, point to freely available software that makes these methods accessible, and note outdated approaches to avoid. A draft reporting guideline is provided, as we believe that a consensus-based reporting standard may facilitate more transparent evaluations of scales. Finally, we argue for a higher bar for calling a measure "valid and reliable": the existence of an original validation paper, often old and based on outdated methods, is not in itself sufficient evidence of validity.

articles.title: Faith in Action: Does Ramadan Reduce Crime?
articles.abstract: As a social institution, religion creates incentives or disincentives for ‘appropriate’ and ‘inappropriate’ social behaviour, including attitudes towards participation in criminal activities. The size of such an effect depends on the intensity of socio-religious norms regarding specific forms of crime. Ramadan, a period of heightened religiosity among Muslims, involves expectations regarding socially desirable behaviour among individuals. Ramadan also involves mandated fasting, which affects local economic activity. How do such expectations and religious restructuring of daily life affect the incidence of crime among believers directly and/or indirectly? Using a difference-in-differences methodology and information from a unique dataset of criminal offences, we estimate the impact of Ramadan on criminal offences committed by those affected by it. Our identification strategy leverages the shifting timing of Ramadan through the Gregorian calendar to isolate the causal effect from confounding seasonality. We find that Ramadan leads to economically and statistically significant reductions in both violent and non-violent crimes, with estimated effect sizes ranging from 8 to 23 percent. We find suggestive evidence of these results being mediated by changes in religiosity and associated behavioural norms rather than by labour market channels. Our results provide suggestive evidence that informal institutions, such as religion, may complement formal state institutions in efforts to reduce crime.

articles.title: Mental Representations Beyond Survey Responses: Evidence from Gendered Wording
articles.authors: Nora Müller, Lynn-Malou Lutz, Oshrat	Hochman, Lisa Hummel Jäckel
articles.abstract: This study examines the effects of different gender formulations on respondents mental representations of the people referred to in survey questions, responses to survey questions, and conventional indicators of questionnaire quality. Using data from a cognitive pretest (N = 466), we compare the generic masculine that is, the use of masculine role nouns to refer to people regardless of gender, which remains common in German surveys with a gender-inclusive formulation using the gender colon and a gender-inclusive neutral formulation. The results show that the linguistic formulation used in survey items significantly affects respondents mental representations of the people referred to in the survey questions. Compared with both gender-inclusive formulations, the generic masculine leads to a substantially lower likelihood that respondents include women in their mental representations. Although wording substantially affected respondents mental representations, responses differed modestly but significantly across wording conditions only for the politician competence item, whereas responses to the income question remained stable across wording conditions. Likewise, neither perceived readability nor response times differed systematically between wording conditions. These findings suggest that relying solely on conventional indicators of survey quality may overlook meaningful differences in the reference groups respondents have in mind when answering survey questions, even when observable survey responses remain largely unchanged. Overall, the findings demonstrate the value of considering respondents’ mental representations alongside conventional indicators of questionnaire quality when evaluating alternative questionnaire formulations, as conventional survey outcomes alone may overlook meaningful cognitive differences between wording conditions.

articles.title: Same Sullivan, different worlds: When prevalence is not health, and lifetables are not mortality
articles.authors: Tim Riffe, Rustam Tursun-zade, Octavio Bramajo
articles.abstract: Background: A lifetable combined with the prevalence of a health condition is sufficient to estimate health expectancy (HLE) using the Sullivan method. Different approaches exist for decomposing differences in HLE calculated this way. It has been suggested that such results cannot be interpreted directly, as they do not adequately disentangle health and mortality effects, with each estimated component potentially reflecting unobserved contributions from both processes. Objectives: Inspired by Anscombe’s quartet, we introduce a Sullivan analog to show that multistate systems with fundamentally different dynamics can yield identical Sullivan-based summary measures. Methods: We generate 32 multistate scenarios, 16 allowing for recovery (returns) and 16 without recovery, all of which exactly match the same values for prevalence, mortality, and by extension healthy life expectancy. We then perform all 240 valid pairwise multistate decompositions to assess whether differences across scenarios are detectable. Results: As expected, the multistate decompositions yield varied and meaningful effects from individual health and mortality hazards on health expectancy, all of which sum to zero at the margin. The analogous Sullivan decompositions all imply that prevalence and lifetable effects are both zero. Conclusions: These findings suggest that results derived from Sullivan-based decompositions are inherently ambiguous. Such results can be interpreted as prevalence and lifetable effects, but not as health and mortality effects, and interpretation must therefore be approached with caution.

articles.title: Republican, Cosmopolitan, Collective, Threshold: The Political Formations of European Port Cities and Their Democratic Fate
articles.abstract: Port cities across Europe are changing. The docks have been automated, fishing industries have contracted, and the working communities that once organised political and social life around maritime labour have been substantially transformed. This paper asks what these changes mean for the political and social formations that European port cities historically produced. Existing scholarship has established that European port cities constitute a distinctive urban formation, one that developed specific political and social characteristics through centuries of maritime life. The paper examines four recurring political and social formations associated with European port cities: a republican disposition, cosmopolitan pragmatism, collective risk culture, and threshold consciousness. It asks whether these formations are disappearing, taking new institutional forms, or being reworked in ways that preserve their language while changing their democratic substance. The paper focuses on European port cities within the Atlantic, North Sea, and Mediterranean maritime traditions. What is happening to these formations matters not only as a question of urban history, but also as a question of democratic life in contemporary European cities.

articles.title: Cloud Capital's Hidden Thirst: Scope 2 Water and the Geography of US Data Center Electricity

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: Data center operators report water use as a facility-level question, disclosing on-site metrics while omitting the water consumed in generating the electricity they purchase — their Scope 2 water footprint. This paper quantifies that omission at the eGRID-subregion level and traces its consequences for a standardized data center load. Comparing EPA eGRID 2018 against eGRID 2023 on an identical pipeline, I find that generation-weighted national water intensity fell 17.1% over the five years in which data center electricity demand accelerated, but that the decline was uneven: several subregions gaining generation share fell more slowly than the national average, and SERC Virginia/Carolina — host to the largest data center market in the world by inventory — fell only 7.7%, less than half the national pace. Combining eGRID generation data with consumption-basis water coefficients, I estimate a total of 1,350.6 billion gallons of operational water consumption embedded in contiguous-US electricity generation across all end uses in 2023, and show that an identical data center's embedded footprint varies approximately 3.2-fold by grid region under common technology-factor assumptions. I then construct a Water Dependency Index and adjust it by a territorial water-scarcity score built from the World Resources Institute's Aqueduct basin indicators, on the principle that identical consumption imposes different costs depending on where it occurs; the adjusted index ranks SERC Virginia/Carolina first in the nation. No widely adopted disclosure framework requires standardized, location-based reporting of electricity-embedded water. The paper proposes extending location-based Scope 2 carbon accounting, which is structurally analogous, to water.

articles.title: Improving Efficiency in Egocentric Network Surveys: A Reproducible Qualtrics Template from Design to Analysis
articles.authors: Ruizhe Liu, Mark Girson, Christopher McCarty, Eleonora Rossi
articles.abstract: How can researchers collect social network data in the field and laboratory settings without imposing excessive technical or logistical burdens? This work presents an improved and reproducible approach for collecting ego network data with alter–alter ties using Qualtrics and for preparing the resulting data for network analysis. By leveraging built-in functions of Qualtrics, this approach reduces the effort required to construct and administer large sets of alter attributes and alter–alter tie questions. An offline pilot dataset demonstrates that the instrument functions reliably in low-connectivity environments, and an accompanying data-processing workflow converts Qualtrics exports into network data suitable for analysis in R. Together, this approach lowers barriers to field-, and lab- based social network data collection, mitigates limitations associated with limited programming background and unfamiliar network software, and supports more consistent integration of network measures into broader survey-based research across disciplines.

articles.title: Caregiver-centred networks and the sustainability of later-life care: A conceptual framework
articles.abstract: Informal caregiving is central to later-life health, yet research has focused primarily on older adults themselves or on caregivers’ individual stress experiences. Less attention has been paid to the structural and relational conditions that shape how caregiving responsibilities are distributed and sustained over time. Building on the Stress Process Model, this paper develops a caregiver-centred framework that integrates four analytically dimensions of network: received support, perceived support, network diversity, and substitute availability. We conceptualize these dimensions as interrelated components of a dynamic feedback system linking caregiver-centred network properties, caregiver burden, and recipient health outcomes. A central contribution is the formalization of substitute availability, defined as the functional capacity of other actors to assume caregiving responsibilities when the primary caregiver is unavailable or overburdened. The framework also identifies contextual conditions, including gender norms, kinship obligations, and demographic change, that shape how caregiving networks are organized. We discuss how this framework can be operationalized through ego-centred and whole-network methods, and outline implications for public health interventions and future longitudinal research.

articles.title: Influence of Media Modality on Language Learning
articles.abstract: This paper seeks to examine which form of television media, anime or live action, best aids Japanese language acquisition in English speakers. While this study focuses on the Japanese language, the literature review covers similar studies on the effect of media exposure on English, Korean, and Turkish vocabulary acquisition. In this study, participants were randomly sorted into two groups, an anime viewing group and a live-action viewing group, and were given Japanese vocabulary words to translate both before and after a media exposure phase. Participants in the live-action group gained more vocabulary words on average compared to participants in the anime group. Animated TV allows students to learn at their individual skill level and may better benefit beginner language learners since it often includes more frequent words in the lexicon. On the other hand, the higher language complexity in live-action TV makes it more suited towards intermediate language learners. This study demonstrates that L2 (target language) television, particularly live-acted L2 television, is an effective tool for vocabulary acquisition and reinforcement. In language learning environments, students could benefit from L2 television consumption to aid and accelerate L2 language acquisition.

articles.title: An Approach to the Design of Housing for Kathmandu, Nepal
articles.abstract: Totally modern design of housing in Nepal causes problems both in its use and construction. The modern designs have arbitrary spatial layouts that are incompatible with the cultural needs of the users. They require many foreign building materials and skills, making construction problematic. Whereas modern design can improve the performance of buildings in areas of damp-proofing and thermal control, traditional design provides culturally useful spaces. Traditional housing is easy to build but fails in some technical aspects of building. A synthesis of modern and traditional designs is the most suitable approach to housing design in Nepal, and government policy should facilitate it by redirecting education in building technology, by encouraging the production of indigenous materials, by suitable regulatory controls, and by incorporating an optimal design in its own housing projects.

articles.title: Improving Subgroup Inclusion in General Population Surveys with Respondent-driven Sampling
articles.authors: Mariel Leonard, Josua Philipp, Julian B. Axenfeld
articles.abstract: Ensuring adequate representation of population subgroups is essential to providing high-quality social science data. Unfortunately, traditional probability-based sampling methods are increasingly prone to differential nonresponse by population subgroups, resulting in underrepresentation of some groups. We consider the potential of respondent-driven sampling (RDS) to supplement probability-based general population samples in order to address sample bias or improve sample inclusion. We find that for select population subgroups, RDS improves sample representation and reduces relative bias without sacrificing data quality. Furthermore, RDS samples can be fielded more quickly than traditional samples, thereby reducing data collection follow-up costs.
